title: “THAT’S JUST HOW I AM” IS A STRANGE SENTENCE FOR SOMEONE WHO SAYS JESUS IS TRANSFORMING THEM
paragraphs:
“THAT’S JUST HOW I AM” IS A STRANGE SENTENCE FOR SOMEONE WHO SAYS JESUS IS TRANSFORMING THEM
Your personality may explain why certain sins tempt you more easily. It was never meant to become permission to protect what Jesus is trying to change.
There is a sentence Christians say all the time that sounds completely harmless.
Maybe you have said it.
Maybe I have said it.
Maybe we said it five minutes after hurting somebody.
“That’s just how I am.”
I’m blunt. That’s just how I am.
I have a temper. That’s just how I am.
I shut people out when I’m hurt. That’s just how I am.
I don’t forgive easily. That’s just how I am.
I’m impatient.
I’m sarcastic.
I’m controlling.
I’m jealous.
I don’t trust anybody.
I disappear when life gets difficult.
I say things when I’m angry and regret them later.
I hold grudges.
I have always been like this.
That’s just how I am.
And perhaps nobody challenges it because it sounds like self-awareness.
But what if sometimes it is not self-awareness at all?
What if it is surrender in the wrong direction?
What if we have learned to give respectable names to things Jesus came to transform?
There is something deeply strange about standing beneath a cross that announces redemption while pointing toward an unchanged pattern and declaring it untouchable because “that’s just me.”
Because Scripture gives the Christian another sentence.
A far more dangerous sentence.
A far more hopeful sentence.
A sentence capable of dismantling the identity we have built around our wounds, habits, failures, temperaments, defenses, and sins.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:17:
The Greek expression at the heart of that declaration is stunning:
καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis.
New creation.
Not merely improved behavior.
Not religious decoration placed over the same old heart.
Not “the same person, except now I attend church.”
New creation.
And notice where Paul places the miracle.
ἐν Χριστῷ — en Christō.
In Christ.
Christian transformation does not begin with a personality test.
It begins with union with Jesus Christ.

This matters because Christianity is not the announcement that naturally patient people should become slightly more patient, naturally gentle people should remain gentle, and naturally disciplined people should congratulate themselves.
The Gospel is much more radical than that.
Jesus saves sinners.
Jesus forgives sinners.
Jesus gives His Spirit to sinners.
Jesus takes people whose hearts have been shaped by rebellion, wounds, pride, fear, lust, anger, selfishness, bitterness, shame, and unbelief and begins conforming them to His own image.
That means your personality is real.
Your temperament is real.
Your history is real.
Your wounds are real.
Your weaknesses are real.
Your tendencies are real.
But none of them are Lord.
Jesus is.
And that distinction can change everything.
There are things about you that do not need repentance.
Being introverted is not sin.
Being extroverted is not holiness.
Being emotionally expressive is not automatically spiritual maturity.
Being quiet is not automatically humility.
Enjoying solitude does not make someone selfish.
Enjoying people does not make someone needy.
Being naturally cautious is not necessarily unbelief.
Being naturally decisive is not necessarily arrogance.
Christianity does not flatten every believer into the same personality.
Peter did not become John.
Paul did not become Barnabas.
God does not redeem human beings by erasing every distinction He created in them.
But there is a difference between personality and sin.
And sometimes that is exactly where we become uncomfortable.
Because personality can explain why certain struggles may come more naturally to us.
It cannot baptize them.
“I’m naturally direct” may explain your communication style.
It does not excuse cruelty.
“I need time alone” may explain how you recharge.
It does not excuse punishing your spouse with silence.
“I’m very discerning” does not sanctify suspicion.
“I’m passionate” does not sanctify rage.
“I’m confident” does not sanctify arrogance.
“I’m careful with money” does not sanctify greed.
“I’m affectionate” does not sanctify sexual immorality.
“I’m independent” does not sanctify refusing correction.
“I’m sensitive” does not sanctify bitterness.
“I’ve always had trust issues” does not make unforgiveness a spiritual gift.
At some point, every follower of Jesus has to face a frightening question:
Have I confused something Christ wants to transform with something I have decided is simply my personality?
That question hurts because excuses are comfortable.
Repentance is not.
Excuses allow us to remain where we are while feeling understood.
Repentance brings us into the light and says:
“Jesus, even if this has been part of me for years, if You call it sin, I will stop calling it personality.”
Maybe you learned anger from your father.
Maybe nobody in your house apologized.
Maybe affection was rare.
Maybe vulnerability was punished.
Maybe sarcasm became armor.
Maybe controlling everything made you feel safe because your childhood was chaos.
Maybe you learned to leave before people could leave you.
Maybe you became emotionally cold because feeling deeply once cost you too much.
Maybe you became fiercely independent because the people who were supposed to protect you failed you.
Those things matter.
Your story matters.
Understanding how a pattern formed can help us recognize it.
But understanding the origin of a destructive pattern does not require us to make peace with its continued rule.
There is compassion in the Gospel for wounded people.
Enormous compassion.
Jesus is not standing over the bruised places of your life mocking you for bleeding.
But His compassion is too great to simply rename every chain “personality” and leave you wearing it.
He came to set captives free.
And sometimes freedom begins when we finally stop defending the prison.
Paul uses another powerful picture in Ephesians 4.
He tells believers concerning their former manner of life to put off the old self.
The Greek phrase is:
τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον — ton palaion anthrōpon.
The old man.
The old self.
Then comes the language of renewal and putting on:
τὸν καινὸν ἄνθρωπον — ton kainon anthrōpon.
The new self.
Paul's imagery is almost like changing clothes.
Take off what belonged to the former life.
Be renewed.
Put on what corresponds to the new life God has created.
And that means Christianity does not give us permission to lovingly preserve every pattern we brought into Christianity.
Some things must come off.
The lying has to come off.
The bitterness has to come off.
The rage has to come off.
The sexual immorality has to come off.
The pride has to come off.
The malice has to come off.
The manipulation has to come off.
The unforgiveness has to come off.
Not because removing those things earns salvation.
It does not.
We are saved by the grace of God through faith, not by constructing an impressive moral résumé.
But the grace that saves us does not make peace with the sin that enslaved us.
Grace forgives.
Grace restores.
Grace teaches.
Grace changes.
Grace brings us back when we fall.
And grace keeps pointing us toward Jesus.
That is why there is an enormous difference between saying:
“I struggle with anger.”
and saying:
“I’m angry. That’s just how I am.”
The first can be confession.
The second can become an identity statement.
There is a difference between:
“I struggle to forgive.”
and:
“I don’t forgive people who betray me. That’s just me.”
One brings weakness into the light.
The other risks building a fence around it.
The Christian is not someone who never struggles.
Please hear that carefully.
Being transformed by Christ does not mean every weakness disappears the moment you believe.
Sanctification is real, and often painfully gradual.
There may be battles you fight repeatedly.
There may be mornings when the old temptation comes roaring back.
There may be moments when you respond exactly as you promised God you would never respond again.
There may be tears after another failure.
There may be repentance at 2:00 in the morning.
There may be prayers that sound less like sermons and more like:
“Jesus, help me. I did it again.”
The evidence of transformation is not sinless perfection.
The Christian's hope is Christ.
But there is a difference between fighting sin and protecting sin.
There is a difference between falling in battle and signing a peace treaty with the enemy.
There is a difference between saying, “Lord, change me,” and saying, “Lord, You may have everything except this because this is just who I am.”
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needed tonight.
Jesus did not die merely to forgive the person you were while leaving every destructive pattern untouched.
He died and rose again to make you His.
That does not mean personality disappears.
It means personality comes under lordship.
Your boldness can become courage instead of aggression.
Your sensitivity can become compassion instead of resentment.
Your analytical mind can become wisdom instead of endless criticism.
Your leadership can become service instead of control.
Your independence can become strength without becoming isolation.
Your passion can become holy zeal instead of uncontrolled anger.
Your ability to speak directly can become truth spoken in love instead of truth weaponized to wound people.
Do you see it?
Jesus is not necessarily trying to erase the way He wired you.
He is teaching every part of you to bow before Him.
This is why the fruit of the Spirit is so confronting.
Scripture speaks of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.
The Greek word translated “self-control” is ἐγκράτεια — enkrateia.
That is uncomfortable for the person who says:
“I just can't control myself when I'm angry.”
The Spirit of God does not shrug and answer:
“Well, anger is your personality.”
He produces fruit.
Not artificial niceness.
Not Christian theater.
Fruit.
And fruit grows.
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes through pruning.
Sometimes through tears.
Sometimes through painful conversations.
Sometimes through apologizing to people we desperately want to blame.
Sometimes through admitting:
“What I did was wrong.”
No “but.”
No explanation designed to erase responsibility.
No “you made me angry.”
No “you know how I am.”
Just:
“I sinned against you. Please forgive me.”
Do you know how powerful that sentence is?
Some marriages are starving for it.
Some children have waited years to hear it from a parent.
Some parents have waited years to hear it from an adult child.
Some friendships died because neither person would say it.
Some churches have been wounded because leaders found theological language for behaviors they should have simply repented of.
And some of us have become experts at explaining ourselves without ever confronting ourselves.
We know our attachment style.
We know our personality type.
We know our childhood wounds.
We know our triggers.
We know our love language.
We know why we withdraw.
We know why we explode.
We know why we distrust.
We know why we become defensive.
There can be genuine value in understanding those things.
But eventually the Christian must ask a different question.
Not merely:
Why am I like this?
But:
Jesus, what do You want to make of me?
That question changes the room.
Because suddenly your past is no longer the highest authority over your future.
Your father may explain something about you.
Your mother may explain something about you.
Your childhood may explain something about you.
Your betrayal may explain something about you.
Your trauma may explain something about you.
Your temperament may explain something about you.
But none of them gets the final word.
Jesus does.
Perhaps the most heartbreaking version of “that's just how I am” is when the sentence is actually hiding fear.
Because sometimes what we really mean is:
“I don't believe I can change.”
We tried before.
We failed.
We prayed.
We fell again.
We promised.
We broke the promise.
So eventually we turned resignation into identity.
“That’s just how I am.”
But the Gospel speaks directly into that graveyard.
καινὴ κτίσις.
New creation.
Not because you possess extraordinary willpower.
Because you belong to an extraordinary Savior.
The Christian story is not:
“I fixed myself.”
It is:
“Christ found me.”
“Christ forgave me.”
“Christ justified me.”
“Christ gave me His Spirit.”
“Christ is changing me.”
“Christ keeps bringing me back.”
“Christ will finish what He began.”
That keeps us from pride when we grow and despair when growth feels slow.
You are not your own savior.
Jesus is.
And perhaps you need to hear something else.
Repentance is not God asking you to become less yourself.
Sin has already distorted us.
Jesus is restoring us.
The closer we come to Christ, the more our humanity begins to look like what humanity was created to be.
Truthful.
Loving.
Pure.
Merciful.
Courageous.
Humble.
Patient.
Faithful.
Holy.
Free.
Maybe you have been protecting something for years.
Everybody around you knows about it.
Your spouse knows.
Your children know.
Your closest friends know.
Your coworkers know.
And whenever somebody gets close enough to confront it, the defenses rise.
“You're too sensitive.”
“You misunderstood me.”
“That's just how I talk.”
“That's how my family is.”
“I've always been like that.”
“This is just who I am.”
But what if tonight Jesus is lovingly putting His finger on the sentence itself?
What if the question is not whether you have always been this way?
What if the question is whether Jesus has permission to change what you have always been?
Read that again.
What if the question is not whether you have always been this way, but whether Jesus has permission to change what you have always been?
Because the cross means your past can explain you without owning you.
Your failures can humble you without naming you.
Your wounds can affect you without becoming your master.
Your personality can describe tendencies without becoming an excuse for disobedience.
And your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Peter could deny Jesus and still be restored.
Paul could carry the shameful history of persecuting Christians and still become an apostle of grace.
The Gospel does not hide the scandal.
It does something infinitely better.
Jesus enters it.
He redeems.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
The cross does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross shows how serious sin is.
And then it shows how astonishing God's mercy is.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
And because He lives, the sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith does not have to build a permanent home inside yesterday.
Maybe your prayer tonight should be brutally simple:
“Jesus, show me what I keep calling personality that You call something I need to surrender.”
That prayer might hurt.
Pray it anyway.
Ask Him about your anger.
Ask Him about your words.
Ask Him about your pride.
Ask Him about how you treat your spouse when nobody else is watching.
Ask Him about the way you respond when corrected.
Ask Him about the resentment you keep feeding.
Ask Him about the secret habit you keep excusing.
Ask Him about the apology you refuse to give.
Ask Him about the person you refuse to forgive.
Ask Him about the version of yourself you keep defending.
Then remember:
Conviction is not an invitation to run away from Jesus.
It is an invitation to run toward Him.
The answer to discovering sin in yourself is not self-hatred.
It is repentance and faith.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Receive mercy.
Ask the Spirit for power.
Make the apology.
Seek reconciliation where appropriate.
Ask mature believers to walk with you.
Open the Bible again tomorrow.
And when you fail, do not transform grace into permission to quit.
Come back to Christ.
Again.
The beautiful scandal of Christianity is that Jesus already knew exactly whom He was saving.
You did not surprise Him.
The cross was not built for impressive people who had finally mastered themselves.
It was built because sinners needed a Savior.
And the empty tomb announces that sin, shame, death, and your former life do not get the last word.
Jesus does.
So perhaps it is time to retire one sentence.
“That’s just how I am.”
And replace it with something more Christian.
“That's something Jesus is still changing in me.”
Can you feel the difference?
One closes the door.
The other opens it.
One protects the pattern.
The other brings it before Christ.
One says, “Accept my chains.”
The other says, “Jesus, make me free.”
Be honest.
Someone else reading your words may realize they are not the only believer still fighting.
Better yet, read it first for yourself.
Not because you need another saved post collecting digital dust, but because the next time you hear yourself say, “That's just how I am,” you may need to come back and remember:
In Christ, who you have been is not the limit of who He is making you.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, confronting what needs confronting, encouraging you when you are exhausted, and continually pointing you toward Jesus Christ, consider staying close to this work.

Following Gospel Warrior helps you remain connected to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment. Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever you have been praying for to follow too.
It does not.
Not because giving money makes someone more spiritual.
It does not.
And certainly not because God needs our money.
He does not.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and one practical expression of that surrender can be generously supporting Gospel-centered work we believe is bearing good fruit.
And there is something else we want believers to know.

If this ministry strengthens you, helps you open Scripture again, calls you toward repentance, reminds you of grace, or gives you something worth sending to a struggling person at midnight, your support helps that work continue.
Not as religious advertising.
As mission.
A wounded wife who has mistaken emotional walls for strength.
A father who has never apologized.
A daughter carrying bitterness.
A believer secretly convinced they can never change.
A Christian who loves Jesus but has spent years protecting the one room in their heart they refuse to let Him renovate.
Maybe they won't.
Maybe tonight they will stop.
Maybe the Holy Spirit will use one ordinary sentence to expose an extraordinary lie.
Maybe somebody will whisper:
“Jesus… I don't want to stay this way.”
And that is where grace becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus does not merely expose what needs changing and abandon us beside the wreckage.
He forgives.
He restores.
He teaches.
He disciplines those He loves.
He gives His Spirit.
He forms His character in His people.
He picks fallen disciples back up.
He writes resurrection into places we thought were finished.
So bring Him the temper.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the defensiveness.
Bring Him the coldness.
Bring Him the fear.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the habits.
Bring Him the excuses.
Bring Him the sentence you have repeated for twenty years.
Bring Him the person you thought you could never become.
Then place all of it before the One who makes sinners new.
Because perhaps the most dangerous thing you can say about a chain is:
“That's just who I am.”
And perhaps one of the most beautiful things a redeemed sinner can say is:
“That may be who I was, and it may still be where I struggle—but Jesus Christ is not finished with me.”
Because your personality may explain the battlefield.
But it does not get to overrule the King who is transforming you on it.
